     121	```
     122	filter requestBodySize > 0
     123	| stats count(*) as requests, pct(requestBodySize, 50) as p50Body, max(requestBodySize) as maxBody, max(requestBodySizeInspectedByWAF) as maxInspected
     124	  by httpRequest.uri, oversizeFields
     125	| sort requests desc | limit 50
     126	```
     127	
     128	**Not validated with data** (executed, 0 rows; field names from the WAF log format documentation; an absent field gives an empty result or blank column).
     129	
     130	**Interpret:** Most URIs show small bodies. A URI whose `maxBody` is far above its `p50Body` is where large requests concentrate. Compare `maxInspected` with `maxBody`: if inspection stops at the web ACL's body limit while the body is larger, the remainder is not inspected. A non-empty `oversizeFields` means WAF could not inspect all of that component. Empty `oversizeFields` with a large body means the body was inspected in full.
     131	
     132	### QI-08 — Count-mode and non-terminating matches
     133	
     134	**Use when:** you want to know which rules are matching without blocking (Count mode), including rules inside managed rule groups and rate-based rules that never reached their limit action (rate-based rules in Count mode appear in the top-level list; validated on Athena only).
     135	
     136	```
     137	filter @message like /"nonTerminatingMatchingRules":\[\{/
     138	| parse @message /"nonTerminatingMatchingRules":\[\{"ruleId":"(?<countRule>[^"]+)","action":"(?<countAction>[^"]+)"/
     139	| stats count(*) as requests by countRule, countAction
     140	| sort requests desc | limit 50
     141	```
     142	
     143	**Interpret:** The regex matches the first non-empty `nonTerminatingMatchingRules` list in each record, whether it is at the top level or inside a rule-group entry, so a record with Count matches in several places is counted once, under the first. Validated: it surfaces managed rules in Count mode (action `COUNT`). The log also carries an `overriddenAction` for such a match; read a raw record when you need to know what the group's own action would have been. A Count rule with very high volume may reflect heavy traffic from a few sources (for example a load test or shared NAT address), but volume alone does not make it benign. Corroborate with QI-13 (small fixed URI set, stable JA4, steady rate over a long period, no other threat labels) before treating the source as known automation, and still report it. A Count rule that matches mostly the same clients as a later block is a candidate for blocking. No rows means no Count-mode activity.
     144	
     145	### QI-08c — Count-mode matches per client (who is behind a Count rule?)
     146	
     147	**Use when:** QI-08 shows a Count-mode rule with high volume and you need to know which clients produce it.
     148	
     149	```
     150	filter @message like /"nonTerminatingMatchingRules":\[\{/
     151	| parse @message /"nonTerminatingMatchingRules":\[\{"ruleId":"(?<countRule>[^"]+)","action":"(?<countAction>[^"]+)"/
     152	| stats count(*) as requests, count_distinct(httpRequest.uri) as distinctUris, min(@timestamp) as firstSeen, max(@timestamp) as lastSeen by httpRequest.clientIp, countRule, countAction
     153	| sort requests desc | limit 50
     154	```
     155	
     156	**Interpret:** Like QI-08, the regex reads only the first non-empty `nonTerminatingMatchingRules` list in each record, so a record with Count matches in several places is attributed to the first one only. A short `firstSeen` to `lastSeen` span with few URIs is a burst against one endpoint; a long span with a steady rate and a small URI set is a candidate for known automation (corroborate with QI-13). There is no per-5-minute maximum in this form: to compare a burst with a rate limit and name its endpoint, run QI-01 filtered to that client (add `and httpRequest.clientIp = "<ip>"`) with 5-minute bins and `httpRequest.httpMethod`, `httpRequest.uri` added to the `by` list. Each client line names method, URI, requests and the busiest 5-minute count against the limit (threat-hunting B-C). Several rows for one rule means the volume is shared, so a dominant client does not explain the quieter ones.
     157	
     158	### QI-09 — Label frequency
     159	
     160	**Use when:** you need an overview of which labels (managed-rule signals) the traffic carries.
     161	
     162	Logs Insights QL cannot expand an array into one row per element, so count the labels by array position and add the counts per label. Procedure:
     163	
     164	1. Run the label-set query below first. The largest number of `{"name":...}` entries in any returned set is the maximum labels per record, `max`. If the output hit its `limit`, raise the limit before trusting `max`.
     165	2. Run the per-position query for `<pos>` = 0 to `max - 1`. Each position is a full scan of the window, so cost grows with `max`; keep the window narrow.
     166	3. Sum `n` per label name across positions. Ignore the row with an empty `labels.<pos>.name`; it counts records with fewer labels than `<pos>+1`.
     167	4. Get the total with `stats count(*) as total` over the same window and compute shares from it.
     168	
     169	```
     170	stats count(*) as n by labels.<pos>.name
     171	| sort n desc | limit 1000
     172	```
     173	
     174	If any position returns exactly 1000 rows, the list is truncated; narrow the window or filter first and report the truncation. The label-set query:
     175	
     176	```
     177	parse @message /"labels":\[(?<labelSet>[^\]]*)\]/
     178	| stats count(*) as requests by labelSet
     179	| sort requests desc | limit 1000
     180	```
     181	
     182	**Interpret:** A broad label such as a challengeable-request marker may appear on every request and is not by itself suspicious. A specific rule label with a small count that matches a QI-02 sub-rule confirms what that rule saw. The label-set query shows which labels travel together per distinct set; many distinct sets mean small counts per set. Copy a `<focus_label>` exactly as shown for QI-10.
     183	
     184	**Validated:** the positional QL form. PPL (`expand`) and SQL (`UNNEST`) forms do not give per-label counts for log-group queries; do not use them.
     185	
     186	### QI-10 — Which labels co-occur with a focus label?
     187	
     188	**Use when:** you have a `<focus_label>` and want to see whether it travels with other labels, forming a signature.
     189	
     190	```
     191	filter @message like /"<focus_label>"/
     192	| parse @message /"labels":\[(?<labelSet>[^\]]*)\]/
     193	| stats count(*) as requests by labelSet
     194	| sort requests desc | limit 50
     195	```
     196	
     197	**Interpret:** First confirm the `<focus_label>` exists and is spelled exactly as in QI-09; a misspelled label also returns 0 rows. Each row is a complete label set carried by requests that include the focus label; the other labels in the set are the co-labels, and `requests` over the sum of all rows gives the share. A high, stable share for one set across many requests means a composite signature. Sets can differ even for traffic from the same clients (validated). No rows means the focus label never appeared. A set that lacks a co-label does not show the traffic is distinct: a missing co-label can simply mean the other rule never evaluated the request (earlier termination, rule order, or a rule scoped to other methods or paths). Never treat absence of a co-label as evidence about the traffic. To see what a denied client carries, add `and httpRequest.clientIp = "<ip>"` to the filter and drop the label from it.
     198	
     199	### QI-11 — Per-IP request banding (low-and-slow detection)
     200	
     201	**Use when:** you suspect traffic is spread across many IPs to stay under per-IP limits.
     202	
     203	```
     204	stats count(*) as req by httpRequest.clientIp
     205	| fields req, httpRequest.clientIp, (req > 10) * 4 + (req > 5 and req <= 10) * 3 + (req >= 3 and req <= 5) * 2 + (req = 2) * 1 as bandCode
     206	| stats count(*) as ips, sum(req) as totalRequests, min(req) as bandMin by bandCode
     207	| sort bandCode asc
     208	```
     209	
     210	**Interpret:** `bandCode` 0 = 1 request, 1 = 2 requests, 2 = 3-5, 3 = 6-10, 4 = 11 or more per IP. Add the event's focus filter (a rule, label or URI) as a first `filter` line to band only the suspect traffic. A large IP population in band 2 that carries most of the requests indicates deliberate distribution under per-IP thresholds. A few IPs in band 4 carrying everything is a concentrated source, handled by per-IP controls. **Not validated with multi-band data** (executed).
     211	
     212	### QI-12 — Distinct URIs per IP (crawling and scanning)
     213	
     214	**Use when:** you suspect scraping or path scanning and want clients touching an unusually wide range of URIs.
     215	
     216	```
     217	stats count(*) as requests, count_distinct(httpRequest.uri) as distinctUris, sum(action != "ALLOW") as denied by httpRequest.clientIp
     218	| filter distinctUris >= 20
     219	| sort distinctUris desc | limit 50
     220	```
     221	
     222	**Interpret:** A client far above the typical `distinctUris` with a low `denied` count is crawling without being stopped. Logs Insights has no median over groups here; get the baseline by running the same query without the `filter` line and reading a few mid-table rows. Lower the `>= 20` threshold for small sites. `count_distinct` is approximate for large counts. Validated: scanning clients stand out by distinct URIs. With few IPs in the window, read each client's own value rather than a median.
     223	
     224	### QI-13 — Known-automation candidates (top talkers by volume and user agent)
     225	
     226	**Use when:** you need to separate high-volume known automation (load tests, monitors, partner integrations) from suspicious traffic.
     227	
     228	```
     229	parse @message /"name":"(?i:user-agent)","value":"(?<ua>[^"]*)"/
     230	| stats count(*) as requests, sum(action = "ALLOW") as allowed, sum(action != "ALLOW") as denied, count_distinct(httpRequest.uri) as distinctUris, count_distinct(ja4Fingerprint) as distinctJa4, earliest(ua) as sampleUa by httpRequest.clientIp
     231	| sort requests desc | limit 20
     232	```
     233	
     234	**Interpret:** One address with a tool-style user agent, a small fixed set of URIs and a dominant share of traffic is a candidate for known automation, but a user agent is trivially spoofable. Require corroboration before classifying it: a small fixed URI set, a stable JA4 (`distinctJa4` of 1), a steady rate over a long period, and no other threat labels. Even then, still report the source rather than silently excluding it. Low-volume clients with browser or empty user agents that appear in QI-02 are the ones to investigate. `sampleUa` shows one user agent, not all. A client with both `denied` and `allowed` requests is a candidate for the attacker-residue check (QI-19). The `allowed` sum (`action = "ALLOW"`) is not validated; `denied` uses the validated QI-12 form. Compute the share of traffic by dividing a client's `requests` by the total from a plain `stats count(*)` over the same window.
     235	
     236	#### QI-13b — Sensitive-endpoint bursts and per-client peak rates (top talker set apart)
     237	
     238	**Use when:** always on the Mode B fast path and in B-C (mandatory); same question as QA-13b. Two `stats` commands: the first counts per minute, the second takes the peak.
     239	
     240	Endpoint scope (one row per client, method and URI for non-GET requests and sensitive paths):
     241	
     242	```
     243	fields httpRequest.clientIp as client, httpRequest.httpMethod as method, httpRequest.uri as uri
     244	| filter method != "GET" or uri like /(?i)(pay|checkout|card|billing|login|signin|sign-in|logon|auth|signup|sign-up|register|password|passwd|reset|forgot|otp|verify)/

{"id": "765de948-aceb-4d39-a0c6-8b98b1e0054b", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "04ab3ddd-519e-465f-9217-80afd4a6b8e9", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: aws-waf-log-analysis
     3	description: >-
     4	  Use this skill when an investigation describes symptoms on a CloudFront distribution, Application
     5	  Load Balancer or API Gateway API and asks what the root cause is or what happened, even if AWS
     6	  WAF is never named: users, partners, webhooks, scripts or mobile apps get HTTP 403, 405 or 202
     7	  responses, empty responses or a 4xx spike; forms, uploads, reviews or listings are rejected; a
     8	  partner integration fails; requests look suspicious or malicious (SQL injection, XSS, scans,
     9	  bots); or an outage or timeouts hit the front door. It checks whether a Web ACL is in the path
     10	  (and continues the RCA when WAF is not the cause), finds which WAF rule, Anti-DDoS rule or Shield
     11	  Advanced mitigation blocked, challenged or only counted the requests and whether that is a false
     12	  positive, an attack or both, and hunts for threats WAF detected but did not block. Uses WAF logs
     13	  (CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena), metrics and sampled requests; records evidence-backed
     14	  findings, advisory scoped fixes and a threat-hunt report.
     15	metadata:
     16	  author: lkna
     17	  version: "1.0.0"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "Incident RCA"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "AWS WAF, AWS Shield, Amazon CloudFront, Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Athena"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Security, Networking"
     21	---
     22	
     23	# AWS WAF Log Analysis
     24	
     25	Find out whether AWS WAF (including Anti-DDoS rules and Shield Advanced automatic mitigation) caused a front-door symptom, and what it denied (Mode A); or hunt WAF logs for threats, including what WAF detected but did not block (Mode B).
     26	
     27	## Purpose and guarantees
     28	
     29	- **Read-only.** Use only Describe, Get and List calls, plus `logs:StartQuery`/`GetQueryResults`, `athena:StartQueryExecution` (SELECT only, when permitted)/`GetQueryResults`, `cloudtrail:LookupEvents`, `wafv2:GetSampledRequests` and `cloudwatch:GetMetricData`.
     30	- Never run DDL. Never change a Web ACL, rule, IP set, Shield setting, log configuration or any other resource.
     31	- **Advisory.** Describe fixes in prose for a human to review and apply. Never apply them.
     32	- **Single-turn.** Never ask the user a question and never wait for input. Apply "Defaults when input is missing", record every default under "Assumptions", and continue.
     33	- **Never stop on a gap.** A denied call or a missing table moves you to the next source or the degraded path.
     34	- **Exact errors.** Record the exact error code. Call something "not permitted" only on `AccessDenied`/`UnauthorizedOperation`.
     35	  - A cancelled, timed-out or throttled call is retried once, then reported as not completed.
     36	  - A tool refusal such as "service operations are not allowed" means: run the call in a subagent.
     37	- **Records are the deliverable** in both modes (symptoms, observations, findings, gaps, hypotheses); the last message closes them (see "Output").
     38	- **Final output.** Complete as delivered; never ends with a question or an offer. Never call `ask_user` (or any ask tool), not even after the answer to offer follow-up work or a fix: a turn that ends on a tool call loses the answer. Put follow-ups in "Next steps" and end on plain text.
     39	
     40	## Pick the mode from the request
     41	
     42	Inputs: the request text plus any incident or alarm details. A threat hunt needs no alarm. Record the mode under "Assumptions".
     43	
     44	Most requests never name WAF: they describe a symptom on a CloudFront distribution, ALB or API Gateway API and ask for the root cause or what happened. Do D-1 first. No Web ACL in the path: record `WAF_CLEARED` and continue the RCA to the actual cause (A0, "After `WAF_CLEARED`"). Otherwise classify:
     45	
     46	| Request contains | Mode |
     47	|---|---|
     48	| Denial or error symptoms: 403/405/202, empty responses, "blocked", "can't access", rejected forms, uploads or posts, a failing partner, webhook or integration, a 4xx/5xx spike, timeouts, an outage, or an alarm on a front-door resource | **Mode A**, starting with the A0 rule-out |
     49	| Suspicious traffic or hunting language: "malicious", "suspicious requests", "SQL injection", "scan", "attack", "bots", "what happened to these requests", "review WAF logs", "is WAF missing anything", a scheduled or recurring review | **Mode B** |
     50	| Both | Mode A first, then Mode B on the same window, focused on the slice Mode A found |
     51	| Neither, but the incident involves a resource that a Web ACL protects | **A0 rule-out only**; if A0 finds WAF implicated or inconclusive, continue with A1 to A7 |
     52	
     53	Mode A `CORRECT_MITIGATION`: recommend Mode B on that slice, or run it when hunting is in scope.
     54	
     55	## Defaults when input is missing
     56	
     57	Never ask; apply and record the default. Full table: "Defaults when input is missing (full table)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md).
     58	
     59	- **Time window:** Mode A: incident start minus 30 min through now, capped at 24 h; no incident time: last 3 h. Mode B: last 7 days.
     60	- **Web ACL:** every ACL on the resources in the request; none identifiable: all ACLs (both scopes), top 3 by denying volume.
     61	- **Several tables or log groups:** the exact location match with the newest data.
     62	- **S3 logging but no table, or no logging:** don't stop; take the degraded path and report the gap with the advisory fix.
     63	- **Missing permission:** fall back to the next source and name the permission.
     64	
     65	## Discover
     66	
     67	Read [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) for D-1 to D-7 at the start of every run. Never ask for a resource or ACL.
     68	
     69	- **D-1 Resource to Web ACL:** CloudFront `GetDistributionConfig` `WebACLId`; regional resources `wafv2:GetWebACLForResource`.
     70	- **D-2 Read the ACL:** `wafv2:GetWebACL` for rule order, actions, managed groups and versions, `RuleActionOverrides`, Count overrides, scope-downs, custom responses, token domains, immunity times, IP set references, and any `ShieldMitigationRuleGroup_*` rule.
     71	- **D-2b Token posture:** classify P0 (no token-aware rules), P1 (token labels, no or only threshold-based enforcement) or P2 (strict token enforcement); confirm with Q-18.
     72	- **D-3 Log destination:** `wafv2:GetLoggingConfiguration`, including logging filters and redacted fields. Log group: Logs Insights. S3 or Firehose to S3: Athena. None, or a non-S3 destination without a full S3 backup: degraded path.
     73	- **D-4 Find the table or log group:** list tables in **every** Glue database, including `default`, across the Regions in D-4. Write "no table" only after that full listing. Never analyze raw log objects (`s3:GetObject`) as a substitute.
     74	- **D-7 Shield Advanced status:** `shield:DescribeSubscription`, `DescribeProtection` (L7AM status and action), `ListAttacks`/`DescribeAttack`, and `DDoSDetected` in `AWS/DDoSProtection`.
     75	
     76	**Region rule.** For CloudFront scope, the ACL, its logging configuration, its log group and its `AWS/WAFV2` metrics are in us-east-1. Only the Glue table and Athena follow the customer's setup; run Athena in the table's Region.
     77	
     78	## Bind schema and guard cost
     79	
     80	Queries are cited as `Q-NN (QA-NN / QI-NN)`; run the one for the backend from D-3 and D-4. Detail: "Schema binding and cost guards (detail)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md).
     81	
     82	- **Athena:** bind `<table>`, `<req>`, label type and `<pf>` from `glue:GetTable`. The log subagent reads [athena-queries.md](references/athena-queries.md) "Schema binding" and the query sections it runs.
     83	- **Logs Insights:** the log subagent reads [logs-insights-queries.md](references/logs-insights-queries.md) "Conventions" and the query sections it runs.

# Mode A: Access-Denied Triage (including WAF rule-out)

Use this reference when users, partners, scripts or mobile apps are denied access to an application behind AWS WAF, when error rates rise on a WAF-protected resource, or when WAF has to be ruled out during a wider outage. Steps A0 to A7 decide whether WAF caused the symptom, which rule and action did it, whether that is a false positive or a correct mitigation, and the narrowest fix.

**Rules for this mode**

- Read-only and advisory. Never change a Web ACL, rule, IP set, Shield setting or any other resource. Fixes are described in prose (see `remediation-patterns.md`).
- Never ask the user and never wait. When an input is missing, apply SKILL.md, "Defaults when input is missing", record the default under "Assumptions" and continue. The output is final and never ends with a question.

| Step | Action | Run | Exit / branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| A0 WAF rule-out | Answer "could WAF be causing this?" with the cheapest checks first. (1) Is a Web ACL in the request path? Check CloudFront and the regional resources involved. (2) Does the symptom type fit WAF? DNS, TLS, timeout, or connection-reset failures don't, but only when the front-door telemetry shows them (the user's wording is not enough), and a custom WAF response code can make a 5xx look like an app error. (3) Did `BlockedRequests`, `ChallengeRequests`, or `CaptchaRequests` rise for the ACL in the window compared with the prior baseline? Include Shield L7AM and Anti-DDoS signals: `DDoSDetected`, `ListAttacks`. "Change lookups (CloudTrail)." section defines:

{"id": "cc6f1897-2b5a-4c7a-b186-888c58549f06", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "8b4341c2-56a5-41af-ba5e-d2f8ba2db09d", "content": [{"text": "Successfully loaded /aidevops/skills/system/proposing-mitigations/SKILL.md"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "cf49df1c-fed5-4c21-b93f-0fb42bbeafe1", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: aws-waf-log-analysis
     3	description: >-
     4	  Use this skill when an investigation describes symptoms on a CloudFront distribution, Application
     5	  Load Balancer or API Gateway API and asks what the root cause is or what happened, even if AWS
     6	  WAF is never named: users, partners, webhooks, scripts or mobile apps get HTTP 403, 405 or 202
     7	  responses, empty responses or a 4xx spike; forms, uploads, reviews or listings are rejected; a
     8	  partner integration fails; requests look suspicious or malicious (SQL injection, XSS, scans,
     9	  bots); or an outage or timeouts hit the front door. It checks whether a Web ACL is in the path
     10	  (and continues the RCA when WAF is not the cause), finds which WAF rule, Anti-DDoS rule or Shield
     11	  Advanced mitigation blocked, challenged or only counted the requests and whether that is a false
     12	  positive, an attack or both, and hunts for threats WAF detected but did not block. Uses WAF logs
     13	  (CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena), metrics and sampled requests; records evidence-backed
     14	  findings, advisory scoped fixes and a threat-hunt report.
     15	metadata:
     16	  author: lkna
     17	  version: "1.0.0"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "Incident RCA"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "AWS WAF, AWS Shield, Amazon CloudFront, Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Athena"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Security, Networking"
     21	---
     22	
     23	# AWS WAF Log Analysis
     24	
     25	Find out whether AWS WAF (including Anti-DDoS rules and Shield Advanced automatic mitigation) caused a front-door symptom, and what it denied (Mode A); or hunt WAF logs for threats, including what WAF detected but did not block (Mode B).
     26	
     27	## Purpose and guarantees
     28	
     29	- **Read-only.** Use only Describe, Get and List calls, plus `logs:StartQuery`/`GetQueryResults`, `athena:StartQueryExecution` (SELECT only, when permitted)/`GetQueryResults`, `cloudtrail:LookupEvents`, `wafv2:GetSampledRequests` and `cloudwatch:GetMetricData`.
     30	- Never run DDL. Never change a Web ACL, rule, IP set, Shield setting, log configuration or any other resource.
     31	- **Advisory.** Describe fixes in prose for a human to review and apply. Never apply them.
     32	- **Single-turn.** Never ask the user a question and never wait for input. Apply "Defaults when input is missing", record every default under "Assumptions", and continue.
     33	- **Never stop on a gap.** A denied call or a missing table moves you to the next source or the degraded path.
     34	- **Exact errors.** Record the exact error code. Call something "not permitted" only on `AccessDenied`/`UnauthorizedOperation`.
     35	  - A cancelled, timed-out or throttled call is retried once, then reported as not completed.
     36	  - A tool refusal such as "service operations are not allowed" means: run the call in a subagent.
     37	- **Records are the deliverable** in both modes (symptoms, observations, findings, gaps, hypotheses); the last message closes them (see "Output").
     38	- **Final output.** Complete as delivered; never ends with a question or an offer. Never call `ask_user` (or any ask tool), not even after the answer to offer follow-up work or a fix: a turn that ends on a tool call loses the answer. Put follow-ups in "Next steps" and end on plain text.
     39	
     40	## Pick the mode from the request
     41	
     42	Inputs: the request text plus any incident or alarm details. A threat hunt needs no alarm. Record the mode under "Assumptions".
     43	
     44	Most requests never name WAF: they describe a symptom on a CloudFront distribution, ALB or API Gateway API and ask for the root cause or what happened. Do D-1 first. No Web ACL in the path: record `WAF_CLEARED` and continue the RCA to the actual cause (A0, "After `WAF_CLEARED`"). Otherwise classify:
     45	
     46	| Request contains | Mode |
     47	|---|---|
     48	| Denial or error symptoms: 403/405/202, empty responses, "blocked", "can't access", rejected forms, uploads or posts, a failing partner, webhook or integration, a 4xx/5xx spike, timeouts, an outage, or an alarm on a front-door resource | **Mode A**, starting with the A0 rule-out |
     49	| Suspicious traffic or hunting language: "malicious", "suspicious requests", "SQL injection", "scan", "attack", "bots", "what happened to these requests", "review WAF logs", "is WAF missing anything", a scheduled or recurring review | **Mode B** |
     50	| Both | Mode A first, then Mode B on the same window, focused on the slice Mode A found |
     51	| Neither, but the incident involves a resource that a Web ACL protects | **A0 rule-out only**; if A0 finds WAF implicated or inconclusive, continue with A1 to A7 |
     52	
     53	Mode A `CORRECT_MITIGATION`: recommend Mode B on that slice, or run it when hunting is in scope.
     54	
     55	## Defaults when input is missing
     56	
     57	Never ask; apply and record the default. Full table: "Defaults when input is missing (full table)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md).
     58	
     59	- **Time window:** Mode A: incident start minus 30 min through now, capped at 24 h; no incident time: last 3 h. Mode B: last 7 days.
     60	- **Web ACL:** every ACL on the resources in the request; none identifiable: all ACLs (both scopes), top 3 by denying volume.
     61	- **Several tables or log groups:** the exact location match with the newest data.
     62	- **S3 logging but no table, or no logging:** don't stop; take the degraded path and report the gap with the advisory fix.
     63	- **Missing permission:** fall back to the next source and name the permission.
     64	
     65	## Discover
     66	
     67	Read [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) for D-1 to D-7 at the start of every run. Never ask for a resource or ACL.
     68	
     69	- **D-1 Resource to Web ACL:** CloudFront `GetDistributionConfig` `WebACLId`; regional resources `wafv2:GetWebACLForResource`.
     70	- **D-2 Read the ACL:** `wafv2:GetWebACL` for rule order, actions, managed groups and versions, `RuleActionOverrides`, Count overrides, scope-downs, custom responses, token domains, immunity times, IP set references, and any `ShieldMitigationRuleGroup_*` rule.
     71	- **D-2b Token posture:** classify P0 (no token-aware rules), P1 (token labels, no or only threshold-based enforcement) or P2 (strict token enforcement); confirm with Q-18.
     72	- **D-3 Log destination:** `wafv2:GetLoggingConfiguration`, including logging filters and redacted fields. Log group: Logs Insights. S3 or Firehose to S3: Athena. None, or a non-S3 destination without a full S3 backup: degraded path.
     73	- **D-4 Find the table or log group:** list tables in **every** Glue database, including `default`, across the Regions in D-4. Write "no table" only after that full listing. Never analyze raw log objects (`s3:GetObject`) as a substitute.
     74	- **D-7 Shield Advanced status:** `shield:DescribeSubscription`, `DescribeProtection` (L7AM status and action), `ListAttacks`/`DescribeAttack`, and `DDoSDetected` in `AWS/DDoSProtection`.
     75	
     76	**Region rule.** For CloudFront scope, the ACL, its logging configuration, its log group and its `AWS/WAFV2` metrics are in us-east-1. Only the Glue table and Athena follow the customer's setup; run Athena in the table's Region.
     77	
     78	## Bind schema and guard cost
     79	
     80	Queries are cited as `Q-NN (QA-NN / QI-NN)`; run the one for the backend from D-3 and D-4. Detail: "Schema binding and cost guards (detail)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md).
     81	
     82	- **Athena:** bind `<table>`, `<req>`, label type and `<pf>` from `glue:GetTable`. The log subagent reads [athena-queries.md](references/athena-queries.md) "Schema binding" and the query sections it runs.
     83	- **Logs Insights:** the log subagent reads [logs-insights-queries.md](references/logs-insights-queries.md) "Conventions" and the query sections it runs.
     84	- **Probe first, in the log subagent.** The main agent runs no Athena query. On a probe error, take the degraded path.
     85	- **Cost:** prune partitions, start narrow, no unbounded `SELECT *`, at most one `UNNEST` per query.
     86	- **Budget:** about 15 log queries (about 10 on the Mode B fast path). Report queries run and bytes scanned.
     87	
     88	## Run it in AWS DevOps Agent
     89

{"id": "e1635bd4-4b0e-4c09-8c88-3c1259907ff4", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_sHBXUWjn57BlngUi8EhKGn", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Remediation Patterns (advisory)
     2	
     3	These patterns are the advice the agent gives in step A7 of `access-denied-triage.md` and in the advisory mitigations of Mode B. They are **advisory only**. The agent never applies them, never runs a command that changes a resource, and never presents a mutating CLI or API call. Describe the change in prose so that a human can review and apply it with their own change process.
     4	
     5	**How to present a pattern**
     6	
     7	- Pick the **narrowest** pattern that fixes the observed (rule, action) pair. Prefer scoping to one sub-rule, URI and method over a rule-group-wide change, and prefer any scoped change over an Allow.
     8	- Mark each pattern as **reduces** (lowers the impact or frequency but leaves part of the pattern) or **eliminates** (stops the observed pattern for the affected scope), for the specific finding.
     9	- Always include a **Count-first validation step**: deploy the new or changed rule in Count, watch its matches in logs (Q-08 (QA-08 / QI-08), QA-08b for rule-group sub-rules) and `CountedRequests` metrics for a representative period, then switch to the terminating action. A rule placed **after** a rule that blocks can never see the blocked requests (a terminating action ends evaluation), so a later label rule cannot be validated while the earlier sub-rule still blocks; use the label-rule sequence in R-01 for that case.
     10	- Name what a human should confirm before acting (for example, that the excluded client really is the partner, or that the excluded URI cannot carry attack payloads).
     11	- Never recommend loosening a rule for traffic judged `CORRECT_MITIGATION`. Never recommend turning a rule or rule group off as the fix (deleting it, removing it from the ACL, or a blanket Count override of a whole group), nor removing the Web ACL or disassociating it from a resource. Scoped sub-rule Count overrides paired with a label rule (R-01) and the R-08 options with their stated trade-off are allowed.
     12	- Never recommend switching a whole managed rule group, or all of its sub-rules, from Count to Block, or removing its `RuleActionOverrides` wholesale, even when a Count-mode sub-rule shows real attacks (detected, not blocked). Enforcement is per sub-rule, scoped to the affected path and field, with a label-based exception (or a scope-down) for the legitimate pattern, validated in Count first (R-01, "Enforcing a Count-mode sub-rule"). Removing one sub-rule's override is the same as a site-wide Block of that sub-rule: recommend it only when Q-20 showed no legitimate matches for it anywhere.
     13	- Use exact rule and label names as they appear in the logs or `GetWebACL`. Rule names and label names can differ in casing (rule `SizeRestrictions_BODY`, label `awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:SizeRestrictions_Body`); copy labels from Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09), never build them from rule IDs.
     14	
     15	| ID | Pattern | Typical verdict |
     16	|---|---|---|
     17	| R-01 | Override one managed sub-rule to Count, then block on its label with a scoped exception; enforce a Count-mode sub-rule the same way | `FALSE_POSITIVE` or `MIXED` on one sub-rule; a sub-rule in Count that detected attacks |
     18	| R-02 | Size-rule exception for specific URIs | `FALSE_POSITIVE` on `SizeRestrictions_BODY` |
     19	| R-03 | Scope-down statement on the managed rule group | `FALSE_POSITIVE` for one known client |
     20	| R-04 | Correct a wrong entry in a custom block IP set; otherwise an IP-based exception for a verified partner, scoped to the denying rule only (never an Allow rule) | `FALSE_POSITIVE` or `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` for a verified partner (the exception is the last resort) |
     21	| R-05 | Restrict Challenge/CAPTCHA to HTML GETs | `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` |
     22	| R-06 | Client integration (WAF JavaScript or mobile SDK) and `TokenDomains` | `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` |
     23	| R-07 | Block or rate-based rule instead of Challenge on machine-to-machine endpoints | `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` on API endpoints |
     24	| R-08 | Shield L7AM action to Count, or migrate to the Anti-DDoS managed rule group | `FALSE_POSITIVE` or `MIXED` from L7AM |
     25	| R-09 | Anti-DDoS rule group tuning | `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` or `MIXED` from Anti-DDoS |
     26	| R-10 | Rate-based rule from Count to scoped Block | abuse detected but not stopped |
     27	| R-11 | WAF-layer and application-layer mitigations for abuse | `CORRECT_MITIGATION` gaps, token abuse |
     28	
     29	---
     30	
     31	## R-01 - Override one managed sub-rule to Count, then block on its label with a scoped exception
     32	
     33	**When it applies:** one sub-rule of a managed rule group blocks legitimate requests on a well-defined scope (a URI, method, host, client or field content), and the sub-rule is still valuable everywhere else; or a sub-rule in Count detected real attacks and has to be enforced without blocking the legitimate content it also matches.
     34	
     35	**Change (prose):** in the managed rule group reference, add a rule action override that sets only that sub-rule to Count. The sub-rule still adds its label to matching requests. Then add a custom rule **after** the rule group (higher priority number) whose statement is: the request has that sub-rule's label AND NOT (the scoped exception, for example URI path starts with the affected path and method is POST). Its action is Block (with the same custom response, if one was used). Requests outside the exception are still blocked exactly as before.
     36	
     37	**Effect:** eliminates the false positive inside the exception scope; protection elsewhere is unchanged. The exception scope itself loses that one sub-rule's protection, so keep it as narrow as possible.
     38	
     39	**Count-first validation (label-rule sequence):** a Block ends evaluation, so a label rule placed after the sub-rule never sees the requests the sub-rule blocks. Validate in this order:
     40	
     41	1. Override the sub-rule to Count. It stops blocking but still adds its label.
     42	2. Add the label rule with the scoped exception, with action Count. Deploy steps 1 and 2 in the same change.
     43	3. Over a representative window, compare the label rule's matches with all requests that carry the sub-rule's label (Q-08 (QA-08 / QI-08) and QA-08b for the sub-rule's Count matches, Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09) for the label). The label rule should match every labelled request outside the exception and none inside it.
     44	4. Switch the label rule to Block.
     45	
     46	**Reduced-protection window:** between steps 1 and 4 the sub-rule's traffic is counted but not blocked anywhere. Keep that window short: deploy steps 1 and 2 together, use the shortest review window that still covers the application's normal traffic cycle, and schedule step 4 in advance. The Count-first sequence above is the recommendation.
     47	
     48	**Mixed matches inside one blocking sub-rule** (Q-20 split it into legitimate content and attack payloads, verdict `MIXED`): the exception in the label rule is the legitimate part's scope, not the whole path when the path also carries attacks. Write it as: label AND NOT (affected path AND method), plus a second Block rule for label AND affected path AND a match statement for the attack pattern classes Q-20 showed (for example an XSS match or a regex for event-handler attributes on the body field; a JNDI-lookup-with-remote-host regex), described as classes, not literal payloads. Both start in Count.
     49	
     50	**Enforcing a Count-mode sub-rule (detected, not blocked).** When a sub-rule overridden to Count matched real attacks and Q-20 also found legitimate content in its matches (or in a sibling sub-rule's matches):
     51	
     52	1. Keep the group's `RuleActionOverrides` as they are. Never switch the whole group or all its sub-rules to Block.
     53	2. Per sub-rule with attack matches, add a label rule after the group: that sub-rule's label (copied from Q-09) AND the affected path (and method) AND NOT (the legitimate pattern's scope: for example the catalog search terms or the field that carries business text), action Count.
     54	3. A sub-rule whose matches were all legitimate content (for example a body sub-rule that matched only product descriptions on one path) stays in Count, or is enforced only outside that path with the same label-rule form.
     55	4. Over a representative window, confirm the label rule matches every attack request Q-20 found and none of the legitimate ones (Q-08 and QA-08b, Q-20 rerun on the label rule), then switch it to Block.
     56	
     57	Effect: *reduces* to *eliminates* the detected-not-blocked attack part on that path, with no new false positives on the legitimate content. Name in "Verify before acting" that a human should confirm the legitimate pattern's scope with the application owner.
     58	
     59	**Alternative (explicitly labelled, not the default): straight to Block.** When the exception is well understood (one exact path and method, confirmed from Q-03 and Q-04), a human may choose to put the label rule straight into Block in the same change as step 1. This avoids the reduced-protection window, but the risk is that an error in the label rule's statement or exception scope blocks legitimate traffic, or lets attack traffic through, without a Count review first. If chosen, watch the label rule's `BlockedRequests` and the excluded path closely right after the change and be ready to roll back.

     63	## R-02 - Size-rule exception for `SizeRestrictions_BODY` on specific URIs
     64	
     65	**When it applies:** `SizeRestrictions_BODY` in the Core rule set (`AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet`) blocks legitimate large bodies (forms, uploads, large JSON) on specific URIs, while the same clients' other requests are allowed.
     66	
     67	**Change (prose):** apply R-01 to `SizeRestrictions_BODY`: override it to Count, then add a custom rule after the group that blocks on its label (copy the exact label from the logs, for example `awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:SizeRestrictions_Body`) AND NOT (URI path is the affected path AND method is the affected method). Optionally add your own size constraint for the excluded URI (a body-size statement with a limit that fits the application's real maximum) so that the exception does not accept bodies of any size.
     68	
     69	Also check `AssociationConfig.RequestBody` in the Web ACL (D-2). It sets how much of the body WAF inspects for each resource type; the CloudFront default inspection size is 16 KB, and limits differ by resource type. Compare with `requestBodySizeInspectedByWAF` and `oversizeFields` from Q-07 (QA-07 / QI-07): content beyond the inspection limit is not inspected by any rule, so raising the inspection limit (which can affect cost) or handling oversize content explicitly may matter for the excluded URI. Raising `AssociationConfig.RequestBody` does **not** change the `SizeRestrictions_BODY` threshold (8 KB) and never fixes this false positive by itself; it only affects content-inspection rules on the excluded URI.
     70	
     71	**Effect:** eliminates the false positive on the excluded URI and method; with your own size constraint, it reduces rather than removes size protection there.
     72	
     73	**Count-first validation:** follow R-01's label-rule sequence: override `SizeRestrictions_BODY` to Count and add the label rule (and any new size constraint) in Count in the same change; confirm the label rule matches all labelled oversize requests outside the excluded URI and method and none of the legitimate large submissions on it; then switch the label rule (and size constraint) to Block. Size protection is reduced site-wide between the override and the switch, so keep that window short. Count-first is the recommendation; going straight to Block is only the explicitly labelled alternative in R-01 (reduced-protection window), with the risk stated there.

     77	## R-03 - Scope-down statement on the managed rule group to exclude a known client
     78	
     79	**When it applies:** a known, verified client (a partner, a monitoring service, a scheduled job) trips one or more rules in a managed group, and the client can be identified reliably.
     80	
     81	**Change (prose):** add a scope-down statement to the managed rule group reference so that the group evaluates only requests that are NOT from that client. Identify the client with an IP set of its documented egress addresses, or with a header the client controls (for example a shared secret header added by the partner, or a header added by an upstream proxy you own). Prefer the IP set when the addresses are stable; a header can be copied by anyone who learns it, so treat it as a weaker identifier and keep its value secret.
     82	
     83	**Effect:** eliminates the denial for that client. The excluded client gets none of the group's protection, so this is broader than R-01.
     84	
     85	**Count-first validation:** before changing the scope-down, add a Count rule that matches the same client condition and confirm in logs that it matches only the intended client's requests (Q-03 (QA-03 / QI-03) for that rule's population).

     89	## R-04 - IP-based exception for a verified partner, scoped to the denying rule only (use with caution)
     90	
     91	**When it applies:** a partner with fixed, verified egress addresses keeps being denied by one rule, and narrower patterns (R-01, R-03, and for Challenge or CAPTCHA R-05, R-06 and a path scope-down) are not practical. For `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`, R-04 ranks below R-05, R-06 and the path scope-down of the challenge rule: list it last, if at all, and say why (egress addresses change, and the address loses that rule's protection).
     92	
     93	**Change (prose):** use the partner's verified addresses only as an exclusion on the rule that denies it: a scope-down statement on that Challenge, CAPTCHA or blocking rule (or on the managed group reference, R-03) of the form "NOT (source IP in <partner IP set>)", preferably combined with the partner's paths or host (for example "NOT (IP in set AND URI path starts with `/api/`)"), or a label-scoped rule that excludes the set (R-01). Every other rule keeps evaluating the partner's requests.
     94	
     95	**Entry in a custom block IP set (the narrowest fix, before any exception).** When the denying rule is a custom Block rule on a customer-managed IP set and `wafv2:GetIPSet` shows the client's IP inside one entry (access-denied-triage, "Per-client symptoms and IP-set evidence"), the fix is to correct that entry: remove it, or narrow the CIDR so it no longer covers the verified partner, after the owner confirms that the address belongs to the partner and how the entry got there. *Eliminates* the denial for that client; every rule still evaluates it. Validate by checking in logs (Q-21 for the client) that the client's requests are allowed afterwards and that no other client covered by the old entry needs it. Report a similarly named allow or trusted set only as a finding (exists, referenced or not); do not recommend adding the client to it or referencing it from an Allow rule.
     96	
     97	**Never** add the client's address to an IP set that an Allow-action rule references (an existing "allow" or trusted-address set included), and never create such an Allow rule: Allow is terminating and ends evaluation, so every rule after it, including managed rule groups, rate-based rules, Bot Control, Anti-DDoS and Shield L7AM mitigation, is skipped for that address, and a compromised or shared address gets unrestricted access. When D-2 shows an existing Allow rule on an IP set, name it only to say the client must not be added to it.
     98	
     99	**Effect:** eliminates the denial by that one rule for the partner's addresses (and paths); all other protection stays.
     100	
     101	**Count-first validation:** first add the same match (IP set AND paths) as a Count rule and confirm it matches only the partner's traffic (correct addresses, expected paths). List under "Verify before acting" that a human should confirm with the partner that the address list is complete and owned by them, and review the set regularly.

     105	## R-05 - Restrict Challenge/CAPTCHA to HTML GETs
     106	
     107	**When it applies:** a Challenge or CAPTCHA rule hits clients that cannot solve it: API calls, JSON requests, browser fetch/XHR, health checks, partner integrations. This is the first-ranked fix for `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` (with R-06 for clients you control), above any R-04 IP-based exception; never suggest adding the client to an IP set used by an Allow rule (R-04).
     108	
     109	**Change (prose):** narrow the Challenge or CAPTCHA rule (or add a scope-down statement to the rule group that applies it) so that it only applies when all of these hold: the URI path does not start with any API prefix the affected client uses (for example `/api/`, the first and simplest scope-down to name), the `Accept` header contains `text/html`, and the method is GET. Build the exclusion from the affected client's full URI set (Q-03 (QA-03 / QI-03)): every non-HTML path it hits must be covered, including `/` or page paths it calls with a non-HTML `Accept`, not just an API prefix; the `Accept` and method conditions cover those when the path list cannot. For a managed sub-rule with a Challenge action (for example Bot Control `TGT_*`), use R-01's shape: override the sub-rule to Count and apply Challenge in a custom rule after the group on its label with these conditions.
     110	
     111	**Effect:** eliminates the lockout for non-HTML and API requests. Those requests are then no longer challenged, so pair this with R-07 for API endpoints if they need protection.
     112	
     113	**Count-first validation:** for a custom Challenge or CAPTCHA rule, add the narrowed condition as a separate Count rule next to it and confirm it matches the browser page loads and none of the API or non-GET requests seen in Q-05 (QA-05 / QI-05), then replace the rule's condition. For a managed sub-rule, follow R-01's label-rule sequence (a challenge also ends evaluation, so a later label rule cannot see challenged requests until the sub-rule is in Count): override the sub-rule to Count and add the label rule in Count together, review, then switch the label rule to Challenge. The sub-rule challenges nobody in between, so keep that window short as described in R-01.

     117	## R-06 - Client integration for token acquisition, and `TokenDomains`
     118	
     119	**When it applies:** the challenged clients are your own browser single-page application or mobile app, and they must keep passing Challenge or CAPTCHA (for example Bot Control targeted rules or Anti-DDoS soft mitigation).
     120	
     121	**Change (prose):** integrate the AWS WAF client application integration: the JavaScript integration for browser apps (it acquires the token and attaches it to fetch calls), or the AWS WAF mobile SDK for Android and iOS apps. For apps that span several subdomains or domains, set the Web ACL's `TokenDomains` to include every domain that should accept the token, so tokens acquired on one host are not `rejected:domain_mismatch` on another.
     122	
     123	**Effect:** eliminates `TOKEN_MISSING` and domain-mismatch failures for clients that integrate. It does not help third-party scripts or partners you cannot change (use R-05 or R-07 for them).
     124	
     125	**Count-first validation:** with the integration released, check in logs that the clients carry `awswaf:managed:token:accepted` (Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09), Q-05 (QA-05 / QI-05)) while the rule is still in Count or scoped to a test path, before enforcing it widely.

     129	## R-07 - Block or rate-based rule instead of Challenge on machine-to-machine endpoints
     130	
     131	**When it applies:** an endpoint is called by scripts, servers or partners that will never run a challenge, and the endpoint still needs protection.
     132	
     133	**Change (prose):** exclude the endpoint from Challenge and CAPTCHA (R-05), and protect it instead with rules that do not need client cooperation: a rate-based rule with action Block scoped to the endpoint, Block rules on labels from managed groups, or authentication at the API layer.
     134	
     135	**Effect:** eliminates the challenge lockout; reduces abuse risk on the endpoint to what the replacement rules catch.
     136	
     137	**Count-first validation:** run the rate-based rule in Count for a representative period and confirm the limit sits above legitimate peak rates per aggregation key (Q-11 (QA-11 / QI-11) for per-IP rates, Q-13 (QA-13 / QI-13) for top talkers).

     141	## R-08 - Shield Advanced L7AM: action to Count, or migrate to the Anti-DDoS managed rule group
     142	
     143	**When it applies:** Shield Advanced automatic application layer DDoS mitigation blocks legitimate clients, for example blocks that continue after `DDoSDetected` returns to 0 on traffic that matches the pre-event baseline.
     144	
     145	**Change (prose):** these are the documented options. (a) In the Shield Advanced protection for the affected resource, change the automatic application layer mitigation action from Block to Count. Mitigation rules keep matching and can be watched in logs (Q-14b: QA-14b / QI-14b) but no longer block. (b) Migrate from L7AM to the AWS WAF Anti-DDoS managed rule group (`AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet`). The AWS WAF Developer Guide states that from March 26, 2026 the Anti-DDoS managed rule group became the default solution for HTTP request flood protection and supersedes L7AM; existing Shield Advanced customers can keep using L7AM (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-automatic-app-layer-response.html). The rule group offers soft (Challenge) and hard (Block) mitigation with tunable sensitivity (R-09). Do not edit the `ShieldMitigationRuleGroup_*` rule group itself; Shield manages it.
     146	
     147	**Effect:** (a) eliminates the false-positive blocks but also removes automatic blocking during future events, so state that trade-off. (b) reduces false positives through tunable sensitivity and exemptions while keeping automatic mitigation.
     148	
     149	**Count-first validation:** with (a), the Count mode itself is the validation: watch QA-14b / QI-14b during the next event to see what would have been blocked. With (b), add the Anti-DDoS rule group with its rules overridden to Count first and review its labels and matches before enforcing.

     153	## R-09 - Anti-DDoS rule group tuning
     154	
     155	**When it applies:** the Anti-DDoS managed rule group challenges or blocks legitimate clients during events: intermittent lockouts on API paths, or broad challenges of all traffic.
     156	
     157	**Change (prose):**
     158	
     159	- **Exempt non-challengeable paths.** Add exempt URI regular expressions (`ExemptUriRegularExpressions` in the rule group's `ClientSideActionConfig`) for paths that cannot take a challenge (APIs, health checks, partner callbacks). Documented behavior (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/APIReference/API_ClientSideAction.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/aws-managed-rule-groups-anti-ddos.html):
     160	  - The regex is matched against the request's host immediately followed by its normalized URI path, without scheme, query string or fragment (for example `www.example.com/api/orders`). A pattern anchored to the start of the path, such as `^/api/`, never matches.
     161	  - The path is normalized first (empty segments, including a trailing slash, and `.` segments removed, `..` resolved), so `/api/` is evaluated as `/api`.
     162	  - Only `GET` requests are challengeable; the `challengeable-request` label is never added to other methods.
     163	  - Requests that match an exempt regex are not evaluated by `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` or `ChallengeDDoSRequests`, whatever their action overrides. The documentation describes the exemption only for these two challenge rules, so do not assume it exempts requests from `DDoSRequests` (Block).
     164	  - The documented starting point is `\/api(\/|$)|\.(acc|avi|css|gif|jpe?g|js|mp[34]|ogg|otf|pdf|png|tiff?|ttf|webm|webp|woff2?)$`, to be reviewed for the application. Between 1 and 5 regexes are allowed.
     165	  - The `Accept` header is not part of the exempt match. Whether a challenged client can actually show the interstitial still depends on the general Challenge behavior (it is served only when `Accept` includes `text/html`).
     166	- **Use sensitivity-based challenges instead of challenging everything.** `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` challenges every challengeable request while the resource is under attack. Override it to Count so that `ChallengeDDoSRequests` is evaluated (it is evaluated only when the previous rule is overridden to Count), and tune the challenge `Sensitivity` in `ClientSideActionConfig` (LOW matches only high-suspicion requests, MEDIUM matches medium and high, HIGH, the default, matches all suspicion levels) so that only suspected attack sources are challenged. Tune `SensitivityToBlock`, used by `DDoSRequests`, the same way if blocks hit baseline clients.
     167	
     168	**Effect:** exemptions eliminate challenge lockouts on the exempted paths (they lose soft mitigation); sensitivity tuning reduces collateral challenges during events.
     169	
     170	**Count-first validation:** review the rule group's labels (`event-detected`, `ddos-request` with low, medium or high suspicion, `challengeable-request`) in logs (Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09), Q-10 (QA-10 / QI-10)) to see which clients each sensitivity level would hit before changing it. Confirm that the exempt pattern removes `challengeable-request` from the intended paths only.

     174	## R-10 - Rate-based rule in Count that matches abuse: switch to a scoped Block
     175	
     176	**When it applies:** a rate-based rule in Count matches abusive traffic (detected but not stopped), for example card testing on a payment endpoint or credential stuffing on login, seen in Q-08 (QA-08 / QI-08) and `ratebasedrulelist`. A client whose Q-08c burst is concentrated on a payment, checkout, login, signup or password-reset URI qualifies whatever its size; the fix for it is this pattern scoped to that URI (a new path-scoped rate-based rule, validated in Count first, if the existing rule is site-wide). Excluding a known-automation IP from the site-wide rule may be needed before any Block, but it is not the fix for the abuse.
     177	
     178	**Change (prose):** switch the rate-based rule to Block, scoped with a scope-down statement to the abused path (for example the payment or login endpoint) rather than the whole site. Choose aggregation keys that separate abusers from legitimate users behind shared egress: client IP when sources are distinct, the forwarded IP header when a trusted proxy or CDN sits in front, or custom keys (for example a session cookie, an API key header, or IP combined with a header) when many users share one NAT or corporate address. Set the limit from observed legitimate peak rates, not from the abuser's rate.
     179	
     180	**Effect:** reduces the abuse to the rate limit on that path; it does not eliminate low-and-slow abuse below the limit (check Q-11 (QA-11 / QI-11)).
     181	
     182	**Never** recommend switching a site-wide rate-based rule to Block when a known-automation client or a shared egress IP (NAT, corporate proxy) exceeds the limit: that blocks legitimate traffic. Scope it to the abused path, or exclude the verified automation with a scope-down, first. Say so explicitly in the output, naming the client: "Switching the site-wide rate-based rule <rule> from Count to Block is not recommended: it would block <client> (<known automation or shared egress>), which exceeds the limit." List the path-scoped rule for a card-testing or credential-stuffing burst first among the mitigations.
     183	
     184	**Count-first validation:** the rule is already in Count; before switching, confirm which keys exceeded the limit and that none of them are known legitimate automation (Q-13 (QA-13 / QI-13) with corroboration) or shared egress used by many real users (Q-08c (QA-08c / QI-08c) lists the keys per client).

     188	## R-11 - WAF-layer and application-layer mitigations for abuse
     189	
     190	**When it applies:** traffic is judged `CORRECT_MITIGATION` but part of it gets through (detected-not-blocked, Count rules, valid tokens, attacker residue, card testing or credential stuffing), or abuse rides on genuine tokens or on SDK and mobile clients that WAF cannot challenge. Present recommendations under a "Recommended mitigations" heading with two sub-headings, "WAF layer" and "Application layer", and mark each as reduces or eliminates for the observed pattern.
     191	
     192	**WAF layer**
     193	
     194	- Close enforcement gaps: reference firing labels in a Block rule, or change offending rule actions from Count or CAPTCHA to Block, scoped narrowly (geography + endpoint + label) to limit collateral impact. For a managed sub-rule in Count, enforce per sub-rule with the R-01 "Enforcing a Count-mode sub-rule" sequence, with an exception for the legitimate content Q-20 found; never the whole group or all its sub-rules.
     195	- Endpoint and geography-scoped rule: geography AND URI AND an OR of the relevant labels.
     196	- Rate-based rules with appropriate aggregation keys (IP, forwarded IP, or custom keys) for volumetric patterns (see R-10).
     197	- **Attacker residue** (Q-19 (QA-19 / QI-19)): the allowed requests carry no labels, so a rule that matches labels cannot catch them. Match the request component the residue used: for a query-argument residue, a string or regex match statement on query arguments scoped to the affected path, or the managed sub-rule that inspects the query string (for example `LFI_QUERYSTRING` in `AWSManagedRulesLinuxRuleSet`); for a URI-path residue, the matching `_URIPATH` sub-rule or a scoped URI-path match. A `UriPath` rule never covers a query-argument residue. Cover every LFI class the residue showed: relative-traversal patterns (dot-dot-slash and its encodings) do not match absolute-path LFI, so a custom match also needs the absolute-path classes (absolute references to OS process-information and system-configuration directories, and their encoded forms), described as classes in the advisory text, not as literal probe strings. Check in D-2 whether that group is already in the ACL, and validate in Count first. Marked *reduces* unless the Count run shows it matches every residue request.
     198	- Redistributed tokens (Q-16b (QA-16b / QI-16b), or Q-16 (QA-16 / QI-16) without token labels): rate-based rules cannot count distinct IPs per token, so a custom rate rule cannot do this. Use the Bot Control targeted rules that do: `TGT_TokenReuseIp*`, `TGT_TokenReuseCountry*` and `TGT_TokenReuseAsn*` (Low/Medium/High thresholds in `label-reference.md`). Keep the group's own actions as they are and add label rules after it that Block (or CAPTCHA, for browser clients only) on those labels, or on `TGT_ML_CoordinatedActivity*` labels, AND the affected country AND the affected paths. `TGT_TokenReuseIpLow` (more than 2 IPs) also catches legitimate mobile users changing networks: use the Medium or High labels for Block and keep Low in Count for visibility. Start the label rules in Count, compare their matches with the legitimate baseline, then enforce.
     199	- No ASN in the logs: add any ASN match statement in a Count rule (the ASNs from an external lookup of the Q-17 prefixes, or a broad list). `clientAsn` is logged only when an ASN match statement is used, so this adds ASN attribution to the logs without blocking anything.
     200	- Caveat: CAPTCHA is ineffective for non-browser mobile and SDK clients, and blocking on redistributed but valid tokens risks real users behind shared egress addresses. Validate against the baseline first.
     201	
     202	**Application layer** (needed when abuse rides on valid tokens or SDK clients)
     203	
     204	- Progressive or tiered authentication for high-value or search-intensive access.
     205	- Client integrity and app attestation, plus request signing with timestamp validation.
     206	- Token-to-device binding: bind a token to a device fingerprint at issue time and reject mismatches. This is the durable fix for redistributed genuine tokens; the WAF token-reuse rules only reduce it.
     207	- Shorter token lifetimes and forced rotation on suspicious usage; roll out regionally first.
     208	- Card testing on a payment endpoint: velocity limits per card, session, account and device in the payment flow, step-up or CAPTCHA on the payment form for browser users, and the payment processor's fraud controls (*eliminates* when enforced per card and account; the WAF rate rule only *reduces*).
     209	- Credential stuffing or fake sign-ups: per-account lockout and throttling, breached-password checks, and multi-factor authentication or email verification.
     210	
     211	**Decision rule:** if the signature is redistribution of genuine tokens AND the legitimate client is a non-browser mobile or SDK app, WAF-layer controls reduce but do not eliminate the pattern. Recommend application-layer controls as the durable fix, with WAF changes as immediate harm reduction.
